title: A clear mind
hookLine: precept five: refrain from drink and drugs that cloud the mind

lines: BY MIDNIGHT, THE BRAKES GO SOFT.
THE PRECEPT THAT GUARDS THE OTHERS.
cards: You've probably seen it at a wedding or a work party. Somebody who is kind and careful at nine o'clock is, by midnight, telling a secret that wasn't theirs, picking a fight, texting an ex, driving when they shouldn't.
The person didn't change. Their mind got cloudy, and the brakes went soft. The fifth precept is different from the first four.
It isn't about an action that harms someone. It protects the one thing that keeps all the others: a clear mind.

teach.b: In Pali: Suramerayamajjapamadatthana veramani sikkhapadam samadiyami. It's a mouthful, so here it is in pieces. Sura and meraya are distilled and fermented drinks.
Majja means intoxicating. And the key word: pamadatthana, a basis for pamada.

teach.h: PAMADA: THE MIND LOSES ITS GRIP.
teach.b: Pamada means heedlessness, carelessness, the mind losing its grip. So, word for word: I undertake the training to refrain from intoxicants that are a basis for heedlessness.
That's why the Buddhist tradition treats it as the guard at the gate. Take away a clear mind and the other four precepts get much harder to keep.
In a discourse to a young man named Sigala, the Buddha lists the dangers of drinking: money wasted, quarrels, illness, a bad reputation, shameless behavior, and a weakened mind.
Two and a half thousand years later, it still reads like a morning after. Buddhists keep this precept in different ways, and it's fair to say so plainly.
Many lay Buddhists, especially in Theravada countries, don't drink at all. Some teachers and communities read it as never drinking to the point of heedlessness.
Medicine taken as prescribed is not what the precept is about.
And many teachers today point the question wider: what else clouds your mind? The phone at one in the morning. The third hour of a show you didn't choose.
The opposite of pamada is appamada, heedfulness, one of the words the Buddha returned to again and again.
A clear mind isn't grim. It's awake enough to notice what's happening while it happens.

how: Buddhists recite the fifth precept, to refrain from intoxicants that lead to heedlessness, with the other four; many abstain from alcohol entirely, while some communities read it as avoiding intoxication.

o: a deep, calm state of meditation
the drink itself, any kind of alcohol
heedlessness, the mind losing its grip

games.q: match the piece of the fifth precept.
p: heedlessness, the mind losing its grip
heard the list of drinking's dangers

s: the fifth precept is about intoxicants that lead to heedlessness
the Pali names drinks that are a basis for pamada, heedlessness.
every Buddhist community reads the fifth precept exactly the same way
many abstain entirely; some read it as never drinking to the point of heedlessness.
medicine taken as prescribed is not what the precept is about.

games.q: why do Buddhist teachers call the fifth precept the guard at the gate?
o: because it's the most important of the five.
because a clouded mind makes the other four much harder to keep.
because it was the first one taught.
games.why: it protects the clear mind that keeps the rest: the other precepts get harder when the brakes go soft.

practice: Notice how clear the mind is right now, not better or worse: a bright morning mind, maybe, or tired, or buzzing.
Then ask, without judging, what usually clouds you, a drink, a screen, lack of sleep, hurry, a certain mood, and quietly name the one answer that comes.
Return to the breath and notice the mind noticing: that noticing is appamada, the clear part.

wordCard.voice: Pamada. Heedlessness, carelessness, the mind losing its grip: what the fifth precept trains against, guarding the other four.

orig.note: Pali: heedlessness, carelessness; its opposite, appamada, heedfulness, is one of the Buddha's key words.

carryVoice: Your line: keep the mind clear. A clear mind guards the other four. Day one hundred twenty-eight, done.
